About: Relativistic Constant Acceleration

Source

Lecture
15 — Relativistic dynamics (four-acceleration, four-force, equations of motion).
Simulation
Relativistic constant acceleration — guided-inquiry mode.
Concept
Under a constant applied force a relativistic particle's velocity asymptotically approaches c rather than growing without bound, while its energy increases without limit.
Serves
Formulate Newton's 2nd law in Lorentz-invariant form (F = dp/dt, p = γmv); relate relativistic force to changes in four-momentum; see how the geometric speed limit c emerges dynamically from the equation of motion.
Inquiry
Before viewing the graph: what do you expect the v-vs-t graph to look like after a long time?
Misconception
"A constant force means constant acceleration, so velocity keeps increasing forever — there's no speed limit in F = ma." Encoded as prediction choice (A) and as the diverging dashed Newtonian curve.

Welcome toRelativistic constant acceleration

A steady thrust that is never switched off — watch what happens to the speed, and where the energy goes.

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

Guided Inquiry

1 · A thrust that never stops

Let’s begin with a push that never lets up. A body at rest is pushed by a steady force F, never switched off. Newton’s F = ma gives a straight line rising for ever. So what do you think the speed really does?

Now press Play and compare the relativistic curve (solid) with the Newtonian prediction (dashed). How did your guess hold up?

① Shaded: the gap between the two speeds.

2 · Where the work goes

Here’s a puzzle for you. The force never changes and the body never stops moving, so work is done at every instant. Yet late in the push the speed barely changes. What do you think all that work is buying?

Now turn on ② Connect to energy, and you’ll see the γ readout appear beside the energy trace.

3 · Below one-fifth of c

Now let’s come back down to everyday speeds. Cars, rockets and planets obey Newton’s F = ma to superb accuracy. Take the same steady force but stop the record at 0.2 c. How far apart do you think the two speeds are there?

Try it yourself: press ⊙ View low velocity, then Play. The solid curve runs only to 0.2 c and lies almost on the dashed line.

4 · Doubling the force

One last experiment. At F/m = 0.5 c/s the speed reads 0.981 c ten seconds in. Double the force to F/m = 1.0 c/s and start again. What’s your guess? Ten seconds in, the speed now reads…

See for yourself: slide F to 1.0 and press Play, and watch the speed badge pass 0.995 c a third of the way across.

5 · Hyperbolic motion

Let’s put a name to everything you’ve just seen. The speed limit isn’t added by hand: it follows from F = dp/dt once momentum is p = γmv — a steady force adds momentum for ever, but the speed that momentum buys saturates at c while E = γmc² grows without bound. Here a₀ = F/m is what an accelerometer on board would read, the proper acceleration; a worldline at constant proper acceleration is a hyperbola in spacetime, hence hyperbolic motion.

② The Lorentz factor γ is printed beside the energy trace.

The Physics

Relativistic constant acceleration · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

This sim pushes a body from rest with a steady force that is never switched off, and plots its speed and energy against time beside Newton's F = ma prediction. It shows what relativity changes, and why that matters in particle accelerators.

What you'll learn

  • How Newton's second law is written to hold at any speed.
  • How speed and energy depend on time under a constant force.
  • Where Newton's F = ma works well, and where it stops.
  • What changing the force does to speed, momentum and energy.
A body of mass m at rest; a force F is applied and never removed.

What's on screen

  • Relativistic speed (solid cyan, upper panel): v/c, with a badge.
  • Newtonian prediction (dashed grey): v = Ft/m, with a triangle where it leaves the plot.
  • v = c (dashed rose): the line v/c = 1.
  • Energy (solid amber, lower panel): E in mc², with a badge. The dashed line is E = mc².

Units: c = 1 and m = 1. Speeds are in c, F is shown as a₀ = F/m in c per second, and t is lab time in seconds.

See itRun the body from rest at your force. Watch for: the solid trace and the dashed grey line leaving the origin together, then parting.

03

A steady force adds momentum at a steady rate

Relativity keeps Newton's second law in the form F = dp/dt, and changes the momentum to p = γmv.

Force is the rate of change of relativistic momentum.

A constant F acting from rest gives p = Ft, a straight line in time. In the sim's units, p/mc = a₀t/c.

The dashed grey line, v = Ft/m, is therefore also p/m: the momentum the force has delivered, divided by m.

Key idea. A constant force fixes how fast the momentum grows, dp/dt. It does not fix how fast the speed grows.
See itRun the body and follow the dashed grey line. Watch for: the dashed line rising straight and leaving the top of the plot at t = 1.2/a₀ (2.4 s at a₀ = 0.5 c/s), marked by a grey triangle.
04

Why the speed cannot keep up

Solve p = γmv for v, with p = Ft. Write x = p/mc = a₀t/c. Then v/c = x/√(1+x²):

The speed bought by a steady force, from rest.

This stays below 1 however large x gets. The factor γ = 1/√(1−v²/c²) grows without limit as v approaches c, so p = γmv can keep growing while v changes less and less.

v/c against p/mc, for the sim's law. At a₀ = 0.5 c/s, p/mc = 1, 5, 15 are t = 2, 10, 30 s.
F

This slider moves the sim's F slider too.

The lab acceleration is not constant: dv/dt = a₀/γ³, which falls toward zero as γ grows.

See itRun the body to the end of the plot. Watch for: the v badge creeping toward 1 c without reaching it, long after the dashed line has left the plot.
05

Newton's prediction at low speed

At a given time both laws have the same momentum, p = Ft. Newton's speed is p/m. The relativistic speed is p/(γm), so Newton's prediction is too high by the factor γ.

For v well below c, γ ≈ 1 + v²/2c². Then p ≈ mv, and F = dp/dt becomes F = ma.

relativistic speedNewton's prediction at the same ttoo high by
0.2 c0.204 c2%
0.5 c0.577 c15%
0.9 c2.06 c129%

The error is γ − 1. It grows smoothly from zero: no speed switches relativity on.

See itZoom in on the first stretch, up to 0.2 c. Watch for: the solid trace lying almost on the dashed line until it stops at v = 0.200 c.
06

Where the work goes

The force keeps doing work, because the body keeps moving. The work raises the energy E = γmc², and E − mc² equals the work done so far.

Energy from the same solution. For large t, E ≈ Fct.

E and p are linked through the mass, and the mass does not change:

Mostly-plus signature (−,+,+,+), as in Lectures 14–15.
  • The mass m is the same number in every frame. It does not grow with speed.
  • E and p each depend on the frame. The combination E² − p²c² does not, and it equals m²c⁴.
  • What grows is γ, and with it both p = γmv and E = γmc².
See itSwitch on ② Connect to energy and run the body. Watch for: the E and γ badges climbing together while the v badge barely changes.
07

What the force changes

The slider sets a₀ = F/m, and the run depends on the force only through a₀t. Doubling F doubles p at every time. A body of twice the mass under the same F follows the run of half the a₀.

at t = 10 sp/mcvE
a₀ = 0.5 c/s50.981 c5.10 mc²
a₀ = 1.0 c/s100.995 c10.05 mc²

Twice the force gives twice the momentum and almost twice the energy. The speed rises by only 0.014 c.

See itRun to t = 10 s at a₀ = 0.5 c/s, then again at 1.0 c/s. Watch for: each run pausing at 10 s, and the card showing both speeds side by side.
08

Where it matters

Four real beams, from γ = E/mc² (or 1 + K/mc²). γ spans five decades, and v/c stays below 1.
  • Accelerators. A proton in the LHC at 6.8 TeV has γ ≈ 7247 and v/c = 1 − 9.5 × 10⁻⁹, about 3 m/s short of c. Raising the beam energy hardly changes the speed, which is why a collider is rated by energy.
  • Medical linacs. A 6 MeV electron already has γ = 12.7 and v = 0.9969 c. Its energy keeps rising along the machine while its speed barely moves.
  • Old television tubes. A 20 keV electron in a CRT has v = 0.27 c and γ = 1.04, so Newton's p = mv is already about 4% low.
Go deeper: the view from on board

For a force along the motion, the force is the same in the lab and in the body's instantaneous rest frame. So a₀ = F/m is what an accelerometer on board reads, and it stays constant. The sim plots only lab-frame quantities.

The worldline is a hyperbola. τ is the proper time on the onboard clock.
The default run (a₀ = 0.5 c/s) as a worldline, from the formulas. At lab time t = 10 s the onboard clock reads τ = 4.62 s.
09

Summary

In one line. A constant force adds momentum at a constant rate, but the speed that momentum buys is capped by c, so the work goes into the energy E = γmc².

Key points

  • F = dp/dt with p = γmv, so from rest p = Ft.
  • v/c = x/√(1+x²), with x = a₀t/c. It stays below 1, and matches Newton's Ft/m only at low speed.
  • E = γmc² keeps rising, about Fct for large t. The mass stays the same.
  • The force enters through a₀ = F/m. Doubling it doubles p, but barely changes v near c.

Common mix-ups

  • "A constant force means a constant acceleration, so the speed rises for ever." A constant F fixes dp/dt. The lab acceleration is a₀/γ³, which falls toward zero.
  • "The body gets heavier, and that is what stops it." The mass is the same in every frame. What grows is γ.
  • "Relativity only matters near c." γ − 1 is already about 2% at 0.2 c, and grows smoothly from zero.

Things to try on your own

  • Set F to 0.2, 0.6 and 1.0 in turn, pause at t = 10 s and note the v badge each time.
  • At a₀ = 0.2 c/s, press ⊙ and find when the solid trace stops. Check it against t = 0.204/a₀ ≈ 1.02 s.
  • Switch on ② and pause at t = 20 s with a₀ = 0.5 c/s. Compare the E badge with γ = √(1 + (a₀t/c)²).
